newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS - ANI pays price for Holter deal.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS - ANI pays price for Holter deal.

text.p: Heavy engineering group Australian National Industries Ltd on Tuesday paid the price for an "unwise" investment in German environmental engineering group Holter as writedowns plunged the company into a huge loss.
ANI announced a net loss of A$213.19 million on sales of A$1.97 billion for the year to June 30, compared with a profit of A$80.38 million the previous year when sales totalled A$1.86 billion.
The result included an abnormal loss of A$198.55 million, stemming largely from a A$233.55 million writedown of the assets of wholly owned Holter, which ANI first bought into in 1991.
"I think with the benefit of hindsight, it wasn't a particularly wise investment for ANI," managing director Peter Stancliffe told Reuters in an interview.

"When you sit back and look at the strategic implications of it, they went into a business that they didn't know much about and it was 20,000 km away from home in an environment they didn't understand," said Stancliffe, who was appointed managing director eight months ago.
"Really, it was already a mature business when they bought in and about to go into decline," he said.
Holter reported a A$55.17 million operating loss in the year to June 30, compared with a loss of A$4.47 million previously.
Stancliffe said he expected to make an announcement regarding Holter's future by September 30.

Negotiations between German government-owned Saarbergwerke AG and Holter about a possible joint venture were proceeding, but the companies now realised that some parts of the businesses should not be joined, he said.

"We may have to adopt a composite solution where there will be parts of Holter that we will joint venture with Saarberg, parts of Holter that we may joint venture with others, parts of Holter that we dispose of altogether and there could be some that we will keep ourselves," he said.
Responding to the results, ratings agency Standard and Poor's Corp placed ANI's BBB long-term credit rating on creditwatch with negative implications.
"ANI's gearing has been adversely affected by further substantial write-downs in relation to Holter's ongoing difficulties," S&P said in a statement.
Asked if there were more writedowns to come, Stancliffe said: "Not that we're aware of at this stage."
On a brighter note, Stancliffe said he expecte ANI to post improved operating results in the 1996/97 year and said the company expected to resume dividend payments.
ANI did not declare a final dividend, leaving total dividend for 1995/96 at two cents, compared to nine cents last year.
"Economic activity in Australia as far as we can tell looks pretty flat," Stancliffe said.
"However, we expect that we will improve our results, but they won't be on the back of improved activity rather they'll be the result of our own improvement programme," he said.
ANI shares ended one cent lower at A$1.01.
